title: 08. Microservices & Architecture Patterns: Docker
summary: Docker is a platform for building, shipping, and running applications in containers — lightweight, isolated, portable process environments that share the host OS kernel but have their own filesystem, network, and process…
objectives: What is a container, and how does it differ from a virtual machine?
What is a Docker image, and how does layering work?
What is the Dockerfile, and how do you write an efficient one?
How do volumes work, and why are they needed?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Docker is a platform for building, shipping, and running applications in containers — lightweight, isolated, portable process environments that share the host OS kernel but have their own filesystem, network, and process namespace — defined by a declarative Dockerfile, composed into immutable images made of layered filesystems, and standardized by the OCI (Open Container Initiative) so they run identically across any Linux machine.

Before Docker, deploying a service meant coordinating the application code with its runtime (specific Python/Java/Node version), system libraries (libssl, libcurl), configuration files, and OS dependencies — the classic "works on my machine" problem. The deployment unit was a VM (slow to start, gigabytes in size, one service per VM) or an AMI (frozen but heavy), and the environment drift between dev, staging, and prod was the source of countless incidents. Docker solved this by packaging the application and all its dependencies into a single immutable artifact — the **container image** — that runs identically anywhere: a developer laptop, a CI runner, a staging cluster, a production cluster. The image is a layered filesystem (each layer is a set of file diffs, cached and reused across images), built from a declarative **Dockerfile** (a recipe of `FROM`, `RUN`, `COPY`, `CMD` instructions). At runtime, Docker creates a **container** from the image — a process (or group of processes) running in an isolated namespace (its own filesystem view, network stack, process tree, user IDs) on top of the host OS kernel, using Linux cgroups for resource limits (CPU, memory) and namespaces for isolation. The container starts in milliseconds (no OS boot), is megabytes in size (no kernel), and many can run on a single host (high density). This combination — portability, immutability, density, and speed — made Docker the standard unit of deployment for modern applications.

The mechanism rests on three Linux kernel features that predate Docker but that Docker made accessible. **(1) Namespaces** (Linux 2.4.19+, 2002): each container gets its own view of system resources — the mount namespace (its own filesystem root), the PID namespace (it sees only its own processes, PID 1 is its init), the network namespace (its own loopback, its own eth0 with a private IP), the UTS namespace (its own hostname), the IPC namespace (its own message queues), the user namespace (UID 0 inside can map to a non-root UID outside). A container is, from the kernel's perspective, just a process with restricted namespace views. **(2) cgroups** (Linux 2.6.24+, 2008): control groups limit and account for resource usage — CPU shares, memory limits, block I/O limits, device access. A container cannot consume more CPU or memory than its cgroup allows, so noisy neighbors on a shared host are bounded. **(3) Union filesystems** (OverlayFS, AUFS): the image's filesystem is a stack of read-only layers (each `RUN`/`COPY`/`ADD` instruction in the Dockerfile creates a layer), and at runtime a thin read-write layer is added on top. File reads check the top layer first, then walk down the stack; file writes copy the file up to the top layer (copy-on-write). This makes images share layers (the Ubuntu base layer is shared across all Ubuntu-based images, deduplicated on disk and in the registry), and makes container creation instant (no full filesystem copy, just a new read-write layer). Docker did not invent these primitives — it wrapped them in a usable API (`docker build`, `docker run`, `docker push`) and a packaging format (the image, with its layered tarballs and manifest) that became the OCI standard.

The real-world journey that made Docker mainstream started at **Docker, Inc.** (originally dotCloud, a PaaS company). Solomon Hykes and his team open-sourced Docker in March 2013, after building it internally to manage dotCloud's containers. The release was perfectly timed — the industry was struggling with deployment complexity, and Docker's promise of "build once, run anywhere" resonated immediately. Adoption was explosive: by 2014, thousands of companies were using Docker; by 2015, it was the de facto standard for container packaging. **Spotify** was one of the earliest large-scale adopters (2013–2014), migrating from a VM-based deployment (each service on its own VM) to Docker containers, packing many containers per host and reducing deployment time from minutes to seconds. Spotify's engineering blog posts about their Docker migration became canonical references for the industry. **Netflix's Titus** (open-sourced 2017) was Netflix's container management platform, built on Docker, running millions of containers across their AWS infrastructure — Netflix had been an early adopter of cloud and microservices, and Docker gave them the deployment portability and density they needed at their scale. **Google** had been running containers internally since 2003 (Borg), and they contributed the **containerd** runtime (donated to CNCF in 2017) as the high-performance, Kubernetes-native container runtime — Docker's runtime was originally used by Kubernetes, but containerd (and CRI-O) replaced it for performance and simplicity. By 2018, Docker's image format was standardized as the **OCI Image Spec**, and the runtime as the **OCI Runtime Spec** (implemented by runc) — meaning any tool that builds OCI images (Docker, Buildah, Kaniko, podman) produces images that run on any OCI-compliant runtime (runc, crun, kata). Docker the company struggled commercially (Docker Enterprise was sold to Mirantis in 2019), but Docker the technology won decisively — the OCI standard ensures it outlives the company.

The trade-offs of Docker are real, though fewer than for VMs. **Security**: containers share the host kernel, so a kernel vulnerability (or a misconfigured container with excessive capabilities) can affect the host and other containers. VMs provide stronger isolation (separate kernels), but at the cost of slower startup and higher overhead. For most workloads, container isolation is sufficient with proper hardening (drop capabilities, use seccomp profiles, run as non-root, use user namespaces for UID mapping). **Persistent storage**: containers are ephemeral by design — when a container is removed, its read-write layer is gone. Stateful workloads (databases) need **volumes** (mounted host directories or networked storage like NFS, EFS) that persist beyond the container's life. Managing volumes adds operational complexity. **Networking**: containers on different hosts need an overlay network (Flannel, Calico, Cilium) to communicate, which adds overhead and complexity compared to flat VM networking. **Image size and build time**: naive Dockerfiles produce huge images (Ubuntu base + all build tools), slowing builds and pulls. Multi-stage builds (build in one image, copy the binary to a minimal runtime image) and distroless/scratch bases address this, but require discipline. **Operational burden at scale**: running containers in production at scale needs orchestration (Kubernetes, ECS, Nomad) — Docker alone is not enough; the orchestration layer is where the real complexity lives.

The deeper lesson is that Docker is the packaging and runtime foundation of modern cloud-native infrastructure — it solved the deployment portability problem that plagued the industry for decades, and it enabled the orchestration layer (Kubernetes) that runs on top. The teams that succeed with Docker treat the image as an immutable, versioned artifact (built in CI, pushed to a registry, pinned by digest not tag), keep images small and focused (one process per container, multi-stage builds, minimal base), and integrate Docker with the orchestration layer cleanly (the image is the deployable unit; Kubernetes runs it). The teams that struggle are usually the ones that treat Docker as a faster VM (running multiple processes in one container, SSHing into containers, storing state in the container's filesystem) — these anti-patterns break Docker's portability and orchestration assumptions. For any organization deploying more than a handful of services, Docker (or OCI containers in general) is the right packaging unit; the question is not whether to containerize, but which orchestration layer to run them on.

persists beyond container)] Container -->|port mapping| Host[Host port 8080] ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` developer: docker build -t myapp:v1 . | v +----------------------+ | Docker daemon | | reads Dockerfile: | | FROM ubuntu:22.04 |----> layer 1 (base, shared w/ other ubuntu imgs) | RUN apt-get ... |----> layer 2 (packages, cached) | COPY app.py |----> layer 3 (app code) | CMD python app.py |----> layer 4 (metadata, no fs change) | stacks layers -> | +----------+-----------+ | v +----------------------+ | Image: myapp:v1 | (immutable, layered, versioned) | layer 4 (metadata) | | layer 3 (app code) | | layer 2 (packages) | | layer 1 (base OS) | +----------+-----------+ | docker push to registry (Docker Hub / ECR / GCR) | v +----------------------+ | Container Registry | (shared, versioned, pull by digest) +----------+-----------+ | docker pull on production host | v +----------------------+ | Container (running) | | +----------------+ | | | read-write | | (thin layer, ephemeral, gone on remove) | | layer (top) | | | +----------------+ | | | image layers | | (read-only, shared with other containers) | | (read-only) | | | +----------------+ | | process: python | (PID 1 in container's PID namespace) | filesystem: overlay| (UnionFS: mount + pid + net + uts + ipc ns) | network: own eth0 | (network namespace, port mapped to host) | CPU/mem: cgroup | (resource limits enforced by kernel) +----------+-----------+ | v +----------------------+ | Linux kernel (shared)| (containers share host kernel, unlike VMs) +----------------------+ VOLUME (persists beyond container): container /data <-- mount --> host /var/lib/docker/volumes/myvol/_data (or networked: NFS, EFS, GlusterFS) ``` ### Walkthrough 1. The developer writes a Dockerfile describing how to build the image — a base image (`FROM ubuntu:22.04`), package installation (`RUN apt-get install`), application code copy (`COPY app.py /app/`), and the startup command (`CMD ["python", "/app/app.py"]`); each instruction creates a new layer, and Docker caches layers so unchanged steps skip rebuilding. 2. The `docker build` command stacks the layers into an immutable image tagged `myapp:v1` (and by digest for immutability), which is pushed to a container registry (Docker Hub, ECR, GCR); the registry stores layers deduplicated across images, so the Ubuntu base layer is shared by all Ubuntu-based images. 3. On the production host, `docker pull` fetches the image (only the layers not already present), and `docker run` creates a container — a new read-write layer on top of the image's read-only layers, plus a PID namespace (the process sees itself as PID 1), a network namespace (its own eth0 with a private IP, port-mapped to the host), a mount namespace (the overlay filesystem), and cgroup limits (CPU and memory caps); the container starts in milliseconds, and a volume can be mounted for data that must persist beyond the container's life.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- One read-only layer of an image.
- An immutable image: a stack of read-only layers + metadata.
- A running instance of an image.
- Manages images, containers, volumes on one host.
- Docker daemon + container lifecycle mock: demonstrates image layering,
- Container creation (namespaces, cgroups), run/stop/remove, and volumes.
- Image digest = hash of all layer digests (immutable identifier)
- Copy-on-write: writes go to the rw layer, not the image

**Defines:** `ImageLayer`, `Image`, `Container`, `DockerDaemon`

```python
# Docker daemon + container lifecycle mock: demonstrates image layering,
# container creation (namespaces, cgroups), run/stop/remove, and volumes.
import os, time, hashlib

class ImageLayer:
    """One read-only layer of an image. Identified by content hash (sha256)."""
    def __init__(self, instruction, content_size_mb):
        self.instruction = instruction
        self.content = b"x" * (content_size_mb * 1024 * 1024)  # simulated
        self.digest = "sha256:" + hashlib.sha256(
            (instruction + str(content_size_mb)).encode()).hexdigest()[:12]
    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Layer({self.instruction}, {self.digest})"

class Image:
    """An immutable image: a stack of read-only layers + metadata."""
    def __init__(self, name, tag, layers, cmd):
        self.name, self.tag, self.layers, self.cmd = name, tag, layers, cmd
        # Image digest = hash of all layer digests (immutable identifier)
        h = hashlib.sha256()
        for l in layers:
            h.update(l.digest.encode())
        self.digest = "sha256:" + h.hexdigest()[:12]
    def size_mb(self):
        return sum(len(l.content) for l in layers) // (1024 * 1024)

class Container:
    """A running instance of an image. Has a read-write layer + isolation."""
    def __init__(self, name, image, volumes=None, cpu_limit=1.0, mem_mb=512):
        self.name, self.image = name, image
        self.rw_layer = []  # copy-on-write changes (ephemeral)
        self.volumes = volumes or {}  # {container_path: host_path}
        self.cpu_limit, self.mem_mb = cpu_limit, mem_mb
        self.pid = None  # would be the PID in the container's PID namespace
        self.ip = f"172.17.0.{hash(name) % 250 + 2}"  # network namespace IP
        self.status = "created"
    def start(self):
        self.pid = hash(self.name) % 30000 + 1000  # simulated PID 1
        self.status = "running"
        print(f"  [container] {self.name} started: pid={self.pid} "
              f"ip={self.ip} cmd={self.image.cmd} cpu={self.cpu_limit} "
              f"mem={self.mem_mb}MB volumes={self.volumes}")
    def stop(self):
        self.status = "stopped"
        print(f"  [container] {self.name} stopped (rw layer discarded on remove)")
    def write_file(self, path, content):
        # copy-on-write: writes go to the rw layer, not the image
        self.rw_layer.append((path, content))
        print(f"  [container] {self.name} wrote {path} ({len(content)}B) to rw layer")

class DockerDaemon:
    """Manages images, containers, volumes on one host."""
    def __init__(self):
        self.images = {}     # digest -> Image
        self.containers = {} # name -> Container
        self.volumes = {}    # name -> host path
    def build(self, name, tag, dockerfile_steps, cmd):
        print(f"[build] building {name}:{tag} from Dockerfile:")
        layers = []
        for instruction, size in dockerfile_steps:
            layer = ImageLayer(instruction, size)
            layers.append(layer)
            print(f"  {instruction:30s} -> {layer.digest} ({size}MB)")
        img = Image(name, tag, layers, cmd)
        self.images[img.digest] = img
        print(f"[build] image {name}:{tag} built: digest={img.digest} "
              f"size={img.size_mb()}MB layers={len(layers)}")
        return img
    def create_volume(self, name):
        path = f"/var/lib/docker/volumes/{name}/_data"
        self.volumes[name] = path
        print(f"[volume] created {name} at {path}")
        return path
    def run(self, name, image, volumes=None, cpu=1.0, mem=512):
        c = Container(name, image, volumes, cpu, mem)
        self.containers[name] = c
        c.start()
        return c
    def remove(self, name):
        c = self.containers.pop(name)
        print(f"[remove] {name}: rw layer discarded, "
              f"volumes ({c.volumes}) persist on host")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    d = DockerDaemon()
    # Dockerfile: each step is (instruction, layer_size_mb)
    img = d.build("myapp", "v1", [
        ("FROM ubuntu:22.04", 80),       # layer 1: base OS
        ("RUN apt-get install python3", 40),  # layer 2: packages
        ("COPY app.py /app/", 5),        # layer 3: app code
    ], cmd=["python3", "/app/app.py"])
    vol = d.create_volume("app-data")
    c1 = d.run("app-1", img, volumes={"/data": vol}, cpu=2.0, mem=1024)
    c1.write_file("/data/log.txt", b"container log entry\n")  # goes to volume
    c1.write_file("/tmp/cache.txt", b"cache")  # goes to rw layer (ephemeral)
    c2 = d.run("app-2", img, cpu=1.0, mem=512)  # second container, same image
    print(f"\n[host] {len(d.containers)} containers running, "
          f"{len(d.images)} image, volumes persist beyond removal")
    c1.stop()
    d.remove("app-1")
    print(f"[host] volume app-data still at {d.volumes['app-data']} "
          f"(survives container removal)")
```
